title: The hospice
hookLine: Cicely Saunders, a Christian nurse and doctor, founds the modern hospice movement

lines: A WARD, A BEDSIDE, MANY VISITS.
WHAT DOES A DYING PERSON NEED?
cards: David Tasma is dying in a London hospital, far from Poland, where he was born, with almost no one to visit him. A hospital social worker, Cicely Saunders, sits by his bed.
Over many visits, they talk about what a dying person actually needs. Not only medicine. Someone to listen.

A place that feels less like a corridor and more like a home. Before he dies, the story goes, he leaves her a gift of money and says he'd like to be a window in the home she builds one day. She doesn't forget it.

teach.b: Cicely Saunders worked first as a nurse, then as a hospital social worker, and then, because she saw that doctors wouldn't listen to her ideas about pain, she trained as a doctor herself.

She was a Christian, and she spoke of her work as a calling. At the bedside she noticed that dying patients were often in pain that nobody was treating well, and lonely in a way nobody was treating at all.

teach.h: TOTAL PAIN: BODY, MIND, FAMILY, SOUL.
teach.b: She came to speak of total pain: the body's pain, yes, but also fear, worry about family, money, and questions about meaning and God. Treat only the body, on her view, and you miss much of the person.
So she founded St Christopher's Hospice in London, a place built for this: careful pain relief, nurses with time, families welcome, chaplains and gardens and windows. Tasma's window was there.
Her conviction came down to something like this: you matter because you are you, and you matter to the end of your life. That's where today's carry comes from. It sits close to some very old words.

teach.h: I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.
teach.b: In Matthew, Jesus tells of a king who welcomes people with these words, in the King James Bible: "I was sick, and ye visited me."

teach.h: TARRY YE HERE, AND WATCH WITH ME.
teach.b: And on his own last night, in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus asks his friends: "tarry ye here, and watch with me." Not fix it. Not explain it.
Watch with me. The hospice is a building where people keep watch.

how: Churches and Christian volunteers visit the sick and dying at home, in hospitals and in hospices, and chaplains of different traditions work alongside hospice nurses and doctors.

o: a place caring for the whole person at life's end
a hospital ward focused on curing serious illness
a clinic where people recover after surgery

games.q: inside the hospice — tap the pairs.

s: Cicely Saunders was only ever a doctor
she was first a nurse, then a social worker, and trained as a doctor so her ideas about pain would be heard.
total pain means only the body's pain
she meant body, fear, family worries and questions of meaning together.
in Gethsemane, Jesus asks his friends to watch with him
"tarry ye here, and watch with me."

games.q: you're a nurse, and you can see dying patients' pain isn't being treated well. the doctors won't listen. what do you do?
o: accept it: it's not your job.
games.why: Cicely Saunders trained as a doctor so her ideas would be heard, and went on to found St Christopher's Hospice.

practice: Think of someone near the end of life, or someone sitting by a bed tonight: a grandparent, a friend who is very ill, a neighbor in a care home; if no one comes to mind, think of the nurses and chaplains keeping watch tonight.
If you pray, hold that person in the words watch with me; if not, keep them company in your thoughts. You don't need the right words.

wordCard.voice: The hospice. A place of care for people who are dying, shaped by Cicely Saunders, a Christian nurse and doctor, around the whole person: body, mind, family and soul.

orig.note: Greek: to keep awake, to watch — "watch with me" in Matthew 26:38.

carryVoice: Your line: you matter to the end. Staying counts, even when the words don't come. Day nine hundred ninety-six.
